stem.text: The function f is differentiable for all x except \( x = \frac{9}{2} \), where it has a jump discontinuity. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 0 < c < 9 \), such that \( f'(c) = - \frac{2}{9} \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(9) - f(0)}{9 - 0} = - \frac{2}{9} \), f is not continuous at \( x = \frac{9}{2} \), which lies in \( \left[0, 9\right] \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[0, 9\right] \) is \( \frac{f(9) - f(0)}{9 - 0} = \frac{13 - 15}{9} = - \frac{2}{9} \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[0, 9\right] \) and differentiable on \( (0, 9) \), but f is not continuous at \( x = \frac{9}{2} \), which lies in \( \left[0, 9\right] \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = - \frac{2}{9} \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(9) - f(0)}{9 - 0} = - \frac{2}{9} \), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be continuous on \( \left[0, 9\right] \).
options.derivation: the Intermediate Value Theorem cited for a claim about the derivative

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(9) - f(0)}{9 - 0} = - \frac{2}{9} \), there is a c with \( 0 < c < 9 \) and \( f'(c) = - \frac{2}{9} \), because an average rate of change is always reached by the derivative.
options.derivation: existence asserted from the arithmetic alone, with no theorem named and no check that one applies
